title: Explorers & Inventions Shorts
chapters: Lewis and Clark: across a continent

units.t: Explorers & Inventions Shorts.
In this episode: Happy accidents: inventions nobody planned, How railways invented time zones and Lewis and Clark: across a continent.
Part one. Happy accidents: inventions nobody planned.
Some of the most useful things in your home began as mistakes, spills and puzzling surprises.
The trick was having someone there who noticed.
The prepared mind.
Louis Pasteur is said to have remarked that chance favours the prepared mind.
Invention is full of examples: a surprising result turns up, most people wipe it away, and someone with the right knowledge stops and asks why.

Accidental discovery is sometimes called serendipity, a word coined in 1754 by the English writer Horace Walpole, inspired by a fairy tale about three princes of Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, who kept making lucky finds.
These stories have been retold many times and sometimes polished.
Each still shows that a lucky moment needed skill and persistence to become useful.
Rubber and X-rays.
Natural rubber was frustrating: sticky and smelly in summer, cracked in winter.
American inventor Charles Goodyear experimented for years while sinking into debt.
By his own account, around 1839 he let a rubber and sulphur mixture touch a hot stove.
It charred like leather but stayed flexible.
This was vulcanisation, named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
Heating rubber with sulphur links its long molecules together, making tyres and seals possible.
Goodyear died in debt.
In November 1895, German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a coated screen glowing near a cathode ray tube he had covered in black cardboard.
He called the unknown rays X.
They passed through flesh but not bone, and one early image showed his wife's hand with her ring.
He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
Microwaves and Velcro.
Raytheon built magnetrons, devices that make microwaves for radar.
The story goes that engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted near one, then aimed the beam at popcorn kernels, which popped.
Microwaves make water molecules in food jiggle, and that motion becomes heat.
Raytheon patented the idea in 1945.
Its first oven, the Radarange, was fridge-sized and expensive.
Affordable home models came in the late 1960s and 1970s.
In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral came back from an Alpine walk with burrs clinging to his trousers and dog.
Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks catching loops of thread.
A strip of hooks and a strip of loops could make a fastener.
After years of work he patented Velcro, from velours, velvet, and crochet, hook.
Copying nature this way is called biomimicry.
A glue that didn't stick.
In 1968, Spencer Silver, a chemist at the American company 3M, was trying to make a very strong adhesive.
Instead he made a weak one.
It stuck to surfaces but peeled off cleanly and could be reused.
Silver found it interesting and spent years promoting it inside the company, but nobody could think of a product.
The answer came from his colleague Art Fry, who sang in a church choir and was annoyed that his paper bookmarks kept falling out of his hymn book.
He realised Silver's glue could make a bookmark that stayed put without damaging the pages.
After testing and false starts, 3M launched Post-it Notes nationally in the United States in 1980.
A solution had waited years for the right problem.
Luck needs hard work.
It is tempting to think great inventions arrive in a flash, but every story here involved long, unglamorous work.
Goodyear experimented for years before his stove moment.
Röntgen spent weeks testing his rays before announcing anything.
De Mestral took more than a decade to turn burrs into a product, and the Post-it took roughly twelve years from odd glue to shop shelves.
Each discovery also depended on someone who understood enough to see that a surprise mattered.
Modern research organisations try to leave room for this by giving scientists time to follow curious results.
The lesson works in everyday life too.
When something goes unexpectedly, ask what it might be telling you.
The key idea: Lucky accidents become inventions only when someone with knowledge notices the surprise and asks why.
Part two. How railways invented time zones.
Once every town set its clocks by its own sun.
Then trains arrived, timetables turned into chaos, and the world had to agree on what time it was.
Trains break local time.
For most of history, time was local.
Noon was when the Sun stood highest, and because the Earth turns, that moment arrives later the further west you go.
Bristol's clocks ran about ten minutes behind London's.
By horse and coach, nobody cared.
Railways changed the scale.
People covered in hours what once took days, and timetables had to be precise to the minute.
With every station on local time, passengers missed connections, and on single track lines confusion over time could cause collisions.
The telegraph made a solution possible, because a time signal could travel along wires almost instantly.
Railway companies became the keepers of the clock and ran their whole networks on one standard time.
Railway time.
In Britain, the Great Western Railway adopted London time in 1840, and by about 1848 most railways used Greenwich Mean Time.
Some towns kept two times for a while, with public clocks given two minute hands.
In 1880 Parliament made GMT the legal time across Great Britain.
North America had a bigger problem: dozens of railway times, with big stations showing several clocks.
On 18 November 1883 the railways of the United States and Canada switched to standard time zones about an hour apart.
In many towns clocks were reset at noon, so people lived through noon twice, which is why it is remembered as the day of two noons.
The railways, not the government, organised it.
US federal law made time zones official only in 1918.
Choosing Greenwich.
Standard zones need a starting point.
In 1884 delegates from about twenty five countries met in Washington DC for the International Meridian Conference.
They chose the meridian through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich as zero degrees longitude.
Practical reasons favoured it, as most of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich.
The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming was one of the great champions of a worldwide system of time based on a single meridian.
Not everyone agreed: France abstained in the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own purposes for decades.
The conference did not impose time zones around the world, but it gave countries a shared reference to build their own on.
Australia's time zones.
In Australia, each colony had kept its own local time, and travellers crossing borders by train faced the same headaches as everyone else.
In 1895 the colonies agreed on standard times based on Greenwich: Eastern, Central and Western.
South Australia first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, but in 1899 moved to nine and a half hours, a choice that has been debated ever since.
The Northern Territory, then administered by South Australia, followed.
Half-hour zones are unusual but not unique: India uses one, and Nepal goes further with a quarter-hour offset.
Daylight saving complicates things today.
Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory don't use it, so in summer the mainland runs on five different times.
Time today.
Greenwich Mean Time has largely been replaced as the world's reference by Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, kept by a network of highly accurate atomic clocks.
Because the Earth's spin is slightly irregular, leap seconds have occasionally been added to keep UTC close to the Sun, but in 2022 international scientists voted to stop adding them by 2035.
Time zones themselves are decided by governments, and politics often beats geography.
China, which spans the width of five standard zones, uses just one official time, so in its far west the Sun can rise very late by the clock.
Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich but uses Central European Time.
The railway engineers' solution still governs every phone and laptop.
The key idea: Each town once kept its own solar noon, and fast trains with precise timetables made that confusing and dangerous.
Part three. Lewis and Clark: across a continent.
In 1804 a small army party set out to cross North America to the Pacific and back.
They found no easy river route, but they mapped a continent and depended on the people who already lived there.
Jefferson's big question.
In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about fifteen million dollars, roughly doubling the young country.
President Jefferson wanted to know what the land held, from plants and rivers to the Native nations living there.
Above all he hoped for a practical water route linking the Missouri to the Pacific.
He chose his secretary, army captain Meriwether Lewis, to lead.
Lewis asked his former army comrade William Clark to share command, and the two worked as genuine equals.
Lewis spent months studying botany, astronomy and medicine and buying supplies, including gifts for Native leaders.
The Corps of Discovery, thirty to forty soldiers and boatmen, with York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, and Lewis's dog Seaman, left near St Louis in May 1804.
Winter, and Sacagawea.
By late 1804 the Corps had travelled over two thousand kilometres up the Missouri to the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in what is now North Dakota, and built a fort to survive the winter.
Only one member died on the whole journey, Sergeant Charles Floyd.
There they hired the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, whose wife Sacagawea was a young Shoshone woman captured by Hidatsa raiders as a girl.
Her baby son travelled with them.
Sacagawea is often pictured as the guide, but she was not hired as one and did not know most of the route.
Her value lay elsewhere: she spoke Shoshone, recognised landmarks near her home, and her presence signalled peaceful intent, since war parties did not travel with women.
In August 1805 the Shoshone chief Cameahwait proved to be her brother, which helped secure horses.
No easy passage.
The first great obstacle was the Great Falls of the Missouri, where it took about a month to carry boats and supplies around a series of waterfalls.
Then came the Rockies.
Jefferson had hoped for a short portage between rivers, but the mountains were range after range.
In September 1805 the Corps crossed the Bitterroot Mountains on a steep trail in early snow, with little game.
They were reduced to eating candles and some of their horses.
Starving and sick, they came down into the lands of the Nez Perce, who fed them and helped them build canoes.
They paddled down the Snake and Columbia rivers and in November 1805 reached the Pacific.
The crossing ended the dream of an easy water route.
A vote on the coast.
The Corps had to decide where to spend the winter, and the captains put the question to the whole party.
York's view and Sacagawea's were recorded alongside the soldiers', an extraordinary moment for an enslaved man and a Native woman in that era, though it changed nothing about their status afterwards.
They built Fort Clatsop, near today's Astoria in Oregon, and endured a wet, miserable winter, with rain on most days.
In March 1806 they started for home.
The return journey included a deadly clash with Blackfeet warriors, the only fight of the journey in which people were killed.
What the journey left.
The Corps reached St Louis in September 1806, after more than two years away, to a public that had largely given them up for dead.
Their journals and Clark's maps transformed knowledge of the west, and they described well over a hundred animals and plants new to science, including the grizzly bear and prairie dog.
But the expedition also opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US government, and over the following century Native nations along the route lost much of their land and many lives.
The travellers' fates were mixed.
Lewis died of gunshot wounds in 1809, widely believed to be suicide.
Clark did not free York for around a decade.
Sacagawea is thought to have died young, around 1812, though some Shoshone traditions say she lived into old age.
The key idea: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to explore the west and find a water route to the Pacific.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do accidents lead to inventions only for some people?
Answer. Someone with the right knowledge asks why.
Question two. Why did local solar time become a problem?
Answer. Fast trains and timetables made differing town times unsafe.
Question three. What did Jefferson most hope the expedition would find?
Answer. A water route linking the Missouri River to the Pacific.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
